summary: EarthTunes turns 43 years of NASA and partner Earth data into music you can explore. Charts of climate data are easy to scroll past. Sound is harder to ignore. We built a data pipeline that combines NASA GISTEMP global temperature anomalies, NSIDC September Arctic sea-ice extent and NIFC U.S. wildfire acreage for 1983–2025. It validates and normalizes the data, and a browser audio engine plays it back as three instrument layers. Warming raises a bright melody, melting ice pulls a low string pad down and wildfire adds percussion. A harmony voice tracks a "tension score" built from heat and ice loss. It moves from a calm C-major chord in the 1990s to tritone and minor-second clusters by 2024, the hottest year on record. A statistics engine finds the record's "Greatest Hits", such as "The Great Melt" (2012) and "Hottest Year on Record" (2024), and writes liner notes for each. Users can play each event, mute layers and follow an interactive timeline. EarthTunes makes climate data accessible to people who learn by listening, including people with visual impairments.
details:
What it does
EarthTunes is a climate sonification web app. Each year of data becomes one musical beat. At normal speed the full 1983–2025 record plays in about 29 seconds.

How it works

  1. Data pipeline (Python): downloads NASA GISTEMP v4, NSIDC Sea Ice Index (G02135) and NIFC wildfire statistics. It cleans them and joins them by year. It checks for missing values, duplicate years, invalid or negative values and out-of-range normalized values, then min-max normalizes each series to 0–1. It exports data.json and a validation report. Known source limitations are documented, for example NIFC's 2004 figures exclude North Carolina state lands.
    • Temperature is a triangle-synth melody from C4 to C6. Hotter years play higher.
    • Sea ice is a sawtooth pad from C2 to C4. Less ice plays lower.
    • Wildfire is noise and kick hits, 1 to 8 per year.
  2. Harmony and tension: tension = normalized temperature × (1 − normalized sea ice). It drives the chord, moving from major triad → minor-major 7th → tritone → minor second → cluster. It also drives detune, distortion and filter brightness, so the music becomes audibly more strained as the planet warms.
  3. Frontend (React + Vite): an interactive Earth hero, a linked climate timeline, a year inspector, filterable Greatest Hits cards and an audio console with play, pause, speed, volume and per-layer mute. The app is deployed on Vercel.

Benefits and impact
EarthTunes reaches people that charts miss: auditory learners, people with visual impairments, students and museum or classroom audiences. Hearing the harmony break down over 40 years makes climate change felt rather than just read about.

Creativity
The music follows the data. The tension in the harmony is computed from it, not added for effect. Ranking events statistically turns raw time series into an album of real climate moments.

Factors we considered

  • Scientific honesty: we document every data limitation, keep raw values next to normalized ones and state that normalization does not imply causation.
  • Geographic mismatch: global temperature, Arctic ice and U.S. fire cover different areas, so wildfire is kept out of the default tension formula.
  • Accessibility, and browser autoplay rules.

Tools used
Python (pandas, requests, pytest), JavaScript, React, Vite, Tone.js, Recharts, Motion, Vitest and Vercel.
